caption:
Dr. Ariel Ostad discusses the Cold-X technology behind Evolysse hyaluronic acid fillers and how it informs his approach to treatment. He shares his perspective on selecting fillers to complement facial anatomy and achieve natural results.

transcript: When we talk about advances in injectable fillers, we tend to focus on what happens when the product is injected. But something that's equally important that happens long before the filler ever reaches the patient, it really happens during the manufacturing process. Evelise is a collection of hyaluronic acid injectables made using something called cold-ex technology. That temperature actually plays in preserving the hyaluronic acid molecule. Hyaluronic acid, otherwise known as HA, is a molecule that occurs naturally within our skin and all our tissues, connective tissue. And one of its important properties is its ability to bind water. But hyaluronic acid is also sensitive to the way it's processed. This is where the key important thing is. Traditional filler manufacturing can involve heat during the cross-linking process and heat can contribute to the breakdown or sort of what we call fragmentation of that hyaluronic acid chains. Cold-ex technology takes really a different approach. It uses near freezing temperature during the manufacturing process. The goal is a filler that's designed to perform better within the treatment area while looking and feeling natural. And within the Evelise collection, we can currently have Evelise form, which has a little more structure. Evelise smooth, which is therefore smoother, and both are made using cold-ex technology. And they have really different, what we call viscoelastic properties, different viscosities. And this way allows us to select a product that's based on the treatment goal. And for me, as a physician and an artist, this is where science really becomes clinically relevant. We're not simply looking at how much volume a filler can create. We're thinking more about the properties of the gel, how it behaves within a dynamic area of the face, and ultimately how that translates into the result we see and feel. Patients today are increasingly telling me the same thing. They want natural results. They don't want to look like they've had filler. They want to remain and maintain their expression. They want to maintain their individuality. They don't want to look different. And that's what makes the science behind cold-ex technology really interesting to me and useful. So it's an innovation to me that really begins at the molecular and manufacturing level. It's designed around something very simple, a natural-looking and a natural-feeling result.

transcript: La crème solaire cause le cancer. Attention, c'est un mythe. Je suis chimiste et je vous explique. title: When to start retinol? #skincare #dermatologist #retinol
transcript: When should you start retinol? If you're thinking about using retinol for anti-aging purposes, there's tons of information out there about how and why it works. But a common question that I get asked all the time is, when should I start? Here is the technical answer. Age 20. I know it sounds super young, but hear me out. Starting at the age of 20, your skin loses about 1% of its total collagen content every single year. And one of the main benefits of retinol is collagen production. So if you're considering retinol for anti-aging purposes, this is technically probably the earliest age that you can start. The reality is, people are using retinoids at a much younger age for conditions like acne and psoriasis. Don't get me wrong, if you're past your 20s, you can still do retinol and derive benefits. Even though the best time to start retinol was in your 20s, the second best time is now.

creator: drarielostad
title: Dr. Ariel Ostad: The Less Is More Approach
caption:
Dr. Ariel Ostad shares his “less is more” approach to cosmetic dermatology. Through precise, individualized treatments, he focuses on enhancing your features, preserving your expression, and achieving natural results.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Visit our official website –
http://www.drarielostad.com/

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Get social with us –

Facebook -
transcript: After more than 30 years of treating patients, one of the things I've come to believe very strongly about is that in aesthetics, less is often more. When a patient comes into my office, my goal isn't to change the way they look. It's to understand what makes their face uniquely theirs and to preserve it. Every face has its own proportions, expressions, asymmetries, and characteristics. Those aren't necessarily things we need to correct. They are part of what makes someone recognizable. So when I assess a patient, I don't start by asking, what can I inject? I ask, what does this patient actually need? And sometimes the answer is very little. Sometimes it's nothing at all. I think we have reached an interesting point in aesthetic medicine where we have more tools available to us than ever before. But just because we can do something doesn't necessarily mean we should. For me, a successful treatment shouldn't announce itself. I don't want someone to walk into a room and have people think she had filler or he had something done. I want people to think, you look great. Maybe they can't even identify why. To me, that's the difference between changing someone's face and refining it. I'm not trying to eliminate every single line. I'm not trying to remove every sign of aging. And I'm certainly not trying to make every patient look the same. Aging to me is part of being human. And my roles to understand where a thoughtful intervention can make a meaningful difference without really taking away the character of the face. That's also why I tend to take really a gradual approach. We can always reassess. We can always enhance later further. We can always do more when it's appropriate. But restraint really gives us the ability to preserve balance, expression and proportion along the way. And after really decades of working with the face, I have developed a tremendous respect for its complexity and really perhaps an even greater respect for knowing when to leave something alone. My philosophy is really simple. Don't chase perfection. Preserve the individual. Use the right treatment in the right place for the right patient and only as much as you truly need. Because ultimately, the best aesthetic work shouldn't make you look like someone else. It should allow you to look like the best version of yourself.
